item.title: How Personal Prayer Promotes Positivity
item.description:
Spirituality

How Personal Prayer Promotes Positivity

This type of prayer can enhance faith, hope, and happiness.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • A significant amount of people embrace personal faith, which includes prayer.
  • Prayer can be an effective coping mechanism in the midst of emotional pain and suffering.
  • The positivity of prayer has been linked to personal, emotional disclosure.
  • Prayer can promote faster recovery from depression and lower rates of suicide.

One of the common practices performed by people of all faith backgrounds, all around the globe, is prayer. Yet depending on religious and theological beliefs, prayer is performed very differently by people of different faith backgrounds. Researchers have studied the positive power of personal prayer, with heartening conclusions.

Source: StockSnap / Pixabay

The Positive Power of Prayer

John David Adams (2026) explored the positive power of prayer by examining the therapeutic influence of self-disclosure.[i] He began by acknowledging private prayer as an activity that, despite statistics of decreased frequency of prayer in the United States over the years, remains a common practice, with 44 percent of American adults reporting that they pray at least once a day, and 23 percent praying weekly or monthly (citing Pew Research Center, 2025). Furthermore, he recognizes that some individuals find private prayer to be an effective coping mechanism in the midst of emotional pain and suffering, and it has even been linked with quicker recovery from depression and lower rates of suicide.

In his research, Adams found that private prayer functions as a beneficial mental health resource and is linked with various measures of well-being, including less depression, more optimism, and higher levels of coping.

Emotional Disclosure Boosts Mental Health

Adams acknowledges that not all forms of prayer are equally effective. He found that a key mediating factor in the positive association between prayer and mental health is emotional disclosure. The participants in Adams’ study were Christian college students who used a seven-day prayer intervention, measuring its impact on anxiety levels. The prayer template included disclosure of feelings to God, along with expressions of confession, adoration, thanksgiving, and supplication. The prayer intervention positively impacted the mental health of the students, including a statistically significant decrease in generalized anxiety—which is important, considering the prevalence of depression and anxiety among young adults.

Adams describes his findings as replicating and extending previous research, establishing private prayer as “an optimal context for the salutary practice of self-disclosure,” contributing to positive mental health. And for people who claim they don’t have time to practice their faith, Adams notes that even brief interventions, such as the one in his study, requiring as little as five minutes a day for one week, produce significant effects.

Personal Faith Produces Positivity

Many people of faith spend much more time praying than five minutes per day. But research reveals that some of the positive benefits of faith-based communion are not solely time-dependent but also linked with the substance of prayer. Thoughtful, intentional personal prayer is a deeper activity than automatically reciting memorized scripts or religious verses that hold no personal meaning. Sharing emotions through prayer yields the greatest results, often supplementing the therapeutic value of sharing thoughts and feelings with trusted loved ones and confidants.

In a world where negativity threatens to erode the peace and positivity of people everywhere, young and old, in every society, sharing emotions during personal prayer is a tried-and-true, research-based approach to restoring faith, hope, and happiness under any circumstance, and in every situation.

item.title: Um, Actually: The Hidden Purpose of Hesitation in Speech
item.description:
Cognition

Um, Actually: The Hidden Purpose of Hesitation in Speech

The surprising function of filler words and pauses.

Posted July 3, 2026

Key points
  • Hesitation words like “um” reflect how the brain plans and produces speech in real time.
  • Speech hesitations aren’t errors, they’re a normal part of how spontaneous language works.
  • Fillers and pauses help us think, speak, and communicate more smoothly.

It happens after almost every high-profile interview or political debate. Before long, social media is full of clips counting the “ums” and “ers”, mocking awkward pauses, or declaring that a speaker “doesn’t know what they’re talking about.” But those tiny moments of hesitation reveal something quite different: a brain working exactly as it should.

Public figures aren't judged solely on what they say, but on how they say it. Politicians, celebrities, and executives alike are criticized for using fillers such as um, uh, and you know, or for pausing while they search for the right words. These hesitation phenomena are often taken as signs of uncertainty, low confidence, or even a lack of intelligence.

That criticism reflects a broader obsession with fluent speech. Countless articles, videos, and public-speaking guides promise to help us eliminate filler words, break the habit of “hemming and hawing,” and sound more polished. The message is that hesitations are mistakes.

In reality, they're anything but. Those tiny pauses and filler words are evidence of a language system working exactly as it should, helping us plan what to say, repair mistakes, and keep conversations running smoothly. (Stollznow, 2026)

Your Brain Is Working Ahead

Speaking may feel effortless, but it's one of the most demanding things your brain does. As we talk, we’re choosing words, arranging them into grammatical sentences, monitoring what we’ve already said, and planning what comes next, all in a matter of milliseconds.

Sometimes that system needs a fraction of a second to catch up. That's where hesitation phenomena come in. These include silent pauses, fillers such as um, uh, and er, as well as expressions like well, actually, you know, and like. We might also repeat a word, restart a sentence, clear our throat, or even laugh nervously while searching for the right expression.

Far from being random noise, these moments give the brain a little extra processing time. They help us retrieve words, plan what we’re going to say next, and sometimes catch and repair an error before it slips out. (Dinkar, 2023)

One way to think of fillers is as the spinning loading icon on a computer. The wheel turns while the computer finishes processing. Likewise, an um or uh signals that the brain is still working, quietly buying itself a moment to transform thoughts into speech.

They’re More Than Empty Words

Hesitation phenomena don’t just help speakers; they communicate something to listeners, too. An um or uh often signals that more speech is coming, discouraging interruptions while the speaker gathers their thoughts. A pause can indicate that someone is choosing their words carefully, discussing something sensitive, or expressing uncertainty. These subtle cues help keep interactions running smoothly.

Not all fillers serve the same purpose. Expressions such as you know can invite agreement or check that a listener is following along. Fillers can also soften uncomfortable silences, making speech feel more natural. Rather than making us sound incompetent, they often make us seem more approachable, conversational, and human.

In everyday speech, hesitation is astonishingly common. Studies have found that speakers produce fillers frequently, regardless of how articulate or experienced they are. (Agmon, et al., 2023) They’re not signs of poor communication; they’re simply part of how spontaneous speech works.

The Myth of Perfect Fluency

The expectation that good speakers should never hesitate is a relatively modern one. We hear polished TED Talks, scripted news broadcasts, and carefully edited YouTube and Instagram videos where every pause has been neatly trimmed away. It’s easy to forget that real conversation is naturally messy.

In fact, completely hesitation-free speech can sound strangely unnatural. If someone never pauses, never backtracks, and never searches for a word, it’s probably because they’ve rehearsed extensively or because an editor has removed every imperfection. Of course, there are situations where excessive hesitation may reflect anxiety or a speech disorder, and persistent disruptions deserve appropriate attention. But for most of us, the occasional um, uh, or thoughtful pause is simply evidence that we’re thinking while we speak.

Language isn’t produced by a machine. It’s created on the fly by an extraordinarily flexible human brain. So, the next time an um or like slips into your speech, don’t be too quick to apologize. These tiny words are reminders that your brain is hard at work, carefully transforming thoughts into language in real time.
